title: Dianthus plumarius

{{Short description|Species of plant}} {{About|the flower|the color|Pink}} {{Speciesbox |image = Dianthus plumarius kz02.jpg |image_caption = ''Dianthus plumarius'', garden pink |genus = Dianthus |species = plumarius |authority = L. }} '''''Dianthus plumarius'''''{{snd}}also called the '''common pink''', '''garden pink''', '''wild pink''', or simply '''pink'''{{snd}}is a [[species]] of flowering plant in the family [[Caryophyllaceae]]. ==Description== [[File:常夏石竹(地被石竹) Dianthus plumarius -上海植物園 Shanghai Botanical Garden- (9180634129).jpg|left|thumb|Close up of flower]] ''Dianthus plumarius'' is a compact [[evergreen]] [[perennial plant|perennial]] reaching on average {{convert|30|-|60|cm}} in height. The stem is green, erect, [[Glabrousness (botany)|glabrous]] and branched on the top. The leaves are opposite, simple, linear and [[sessility (botany)|sessile]], more or less erect and [[flexuous]], with a sheath embracing the stem. They are about {{convert|3|mm}} wide and about {{convert|10|cm}} long. The [[calyx (botany)|calyx]] is a green cylindrical tube about {{convert|2|cm}} long, with reddish teeth. The flowers are radially symmetric, [[hermaphrodite]], gathered in [[scape (botany)|scape]]s of 3–5 flowers, with 10 [[stamens]]. They have five pink petals, {{convert|10|-|15|mm}} long, with fringed margins. The flowering period extends from May through August. The fruits are [[Capsule (botany)|capsules]] with a few seeds.{{Cite web|last=Shoot|title=Dianthus plumarius Pink Common pink Wild pink Clove pink Cottage pink Feathered pink Garden pink Grass pink Indian eye Mary's pink Mother of all pinks Pheasant's eye Scottish pink Care Plant Varieties & Pruning Advice|url=http://www.shootgardening.co.uk/plant/dianthus-plumarius|access-date=2021-09-10|website=www.shootgardening.co.uk|language=en}} ==Distribution== [[file:dianthus-plumarius-hoffman.jpg|right|thumb|Flower atlas print from 1884]] This species is native to [[Austria]], [[Croatia]], and [[Slovenia]], and naturalized in [[Italy]], [[Germany]], and the [[United Kingdom]].{{Cite web|title=Hortipedia - Dianthus plumarius|url=https://en.hortipedia.com/Dianthus_plumarius|access-date=2021-09-10|website=en.hortipedia.com}} In the United States it is known to [[garden escape|grow invasively]] in [[Alabama]], [[South Carolina]], [[North Carolina]], [[Virginia]], [[Pennsylvania]], [[Indiana]], [[Illinois]], [[Missouri]], [[Wisconsin]], [[Michigan]], [[New York State]], [[New Hampshire]], [[Vermont]], [[Maine]], and [[California]].{{Cite web|title=NatureServe Explorer 2.0|url=https://explorer.natureserve.org/Search?sn=Dianthus+plumarius|access-date=2021-09-10|website=explorer.natureserve.org}} ==Etymology== While the origin of the name "pink" is uncertain, within two decades of its 1570 appearance in the written record, that flower's name was being used to refer to the pastel red known as pink in English today. Whether the [[pinking shear]] shares a common origin, or is named after the flower, is uncertain.[http://www.dictionary.com/browse/pink Pink: Etymology – Dictionary.com]
1570s, common name of Dianthus, a garden plant of various colors, of unknown origin. Its use for "pale rose color" first recorded 1733 (pink-coloured is recorded from 1680s), from one of the colors of the flowers. The plant name is perhaps from pink (v.) via notion of "perforated" petals, or from Dutch pink "small" (see pinkie), from the term pinck oogen "half-closed eyes," literally "small eyes," which was borrowed into English (1570s) and may have been used as a name for Dianthus, which sometimes has pale red flowers. ==See also== * [[List of Award of Garden Merit dianthus]] ==References== {{Reflist}} {{Taxonbar|from=Q159590}} [[Category:Dianthus|plumarius]]
